question: What is the main job of hemostasis in the body?

options.C: Preventing excessive blood loss from injured vessels
options.D: Speeding up red blood cell production

explanation: Think of hemostasis as your body's natural emergency repair kit. When a blood vessel gets injured, it kicks in to stop the bleeding and patch things up! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: What happens if the body's clotting system becomes overactive?

options.A: White blood cells are quickly destroyed
options.B: Severe swelling occurs from fluid shifts
options.C: Clots form inside healthy blood vessels

explanation: When clotting goes into overdrive, it can form unwanted clots (thrombi) inside normal blood vessels, which can block blood flow to vital organs like the brain or heart. Moderation is key! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: What causes a blood vessel to instantly spasm when it gets injured?

options.A: Activation of red blood cell proteins
options.B: Direct injury to the muscle and local chemical signals
options.C: Release of heparin from tissue mast cells
options.D: A sudden spike in blood pressure

explanation: When a vessel is hurt, its muscular walls instantly contract (spasm) to narrow the opening and immediately slow down blood loss. Pretty smart design! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the role of exposed collagen fibers when a blood vessel is damaged?

options.A: They release heparin to dissolve micro-clots
options.B: They turn fibrinogen directly into solid threads
options.C: They stimulate rapid division of cells
options.D: They attract and activate platelets to the injury site

explanation: When the inner lining of a vessel tears, the underlying collagen acts like sticky velcro, catching platelets as they float by to start building a plug. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h2)

question: What triggers the extrinsic clotting pathway?

options.A: Release of tissue factor from damaged tissues outside the vessel
options.C: High levels of calcium ions in the blood

explanation: Remember: 'Extrinsic' means outside. This pathway is triggered quickly when tissue factor leaks out from injured cells surrounding a damaged blood vessel. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h3)

question: How does the intrinsic clotting pathway differ from the extrinsic pathway?

options.A: It is slower and starts from inside the blood vessel
options.B: It skips Factor X activation completely
options.C: It relies only on platelet granules
options.D: It is triggered by tissue trauma outside the vessel

explanation: Think of 'intrinsic' as internal. It happens right inside the vessel when blood contacts damaged surfaces, and it takes a little bit longer than the extrinsic route. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the main job of thrombin during the clotting process?

options.A: Activating tissue factor in the vessel wall
options.B: Converting soluble fibrinogen into sticky fibrin threads
options.C: Stopping platelets from clumping too much

explanation: Thrombin is a superstar enzyme here! It takes the floating, liquid fibrinogen and turns it into tough, sticky fibrin threads that form the actual clot mesh. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the main responsibility of Factor XIII in the clotting cascade?

options.D: Cross-linking fibrin strands to create a stable mesh

explanation: Once the fibrin threads are laid down, Factor XIII comes in like a welder, creating strong cross-links to make the clot sturdy and stable. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which substance turns plasminogen into active plasmin to dissolve blood clots?
explanation: Often called tPA, tissue plasminogen activator helps clean up old clots by turning plasminogen into plasmin, the enzyme that dissolves the fibrin mesh when healing is done. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of clot retraction?

options.A: Pulling the edges of the damaged vessel closer together
options.B: Preventing white blood cells from entering the wound
options.D: Speeding up platelet production in the bone marrow

explanation: After the clot forms, the platelets contract, shrinking the whole mesh. This acts like drawstrings, pulling the torn edges of the blood vessel closer for a faster heal! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h5)

question: How does antithrombin III protect the body from abnormal clotting?

options.A: It binds to and neutralizes excess active thrombin
options.C: It triggers vascular spasms in healthy tissue
options.D: It stops platelets from sticking to healthy vessels

explanation: Antithrombin III acts like a safety brake. It catches and shuts down extra thrombin so clots don't form where they shouldn't. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main function of Protein C and Protein S?

options.D: Inactivating specific clotting factors like Factor V and VIII

explanation: Proteins C and S are natural anticoagulants. They team up to turn off certain clotting factors (like V and VIII), keeping our blood flowing smoothly. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which lab test is mainly used to monitor oral Warfarin therapy?

options.C: Bleeding time test using a forearm incision
options.D: Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio (PT/INR)

explanation: When patients take Warfarin (a blood thinner), nurses and doctors track their PT/INR to make sure their blood is clotting at a safe, therapeutic level. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h7)

question: A patient receiving intravenous heparin needs monitoring with which lab test?
explanation: Heparin affects the intrinsic pathway of the clotting cascade, so we use the aPTT test to keep our patient safe and well-monitored. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the underlying cause of classic Hemophilia A?

options.B: Rapid breakdown of the fibrin mesh
options.C: Deficiency or absence of clotting Factor VIII
options.D: Low platelet count in the spleen

explanation: Hemophilia A is an inherited condition where the body lacks enough Factor VIII, making it harder for the blood to form stable clots. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h8)

question: What dangerous paradox happens during Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)?

options.A: A complete lack of thrombin causes internal organ calcification
options.B: Excessive bleeding causes the bone marrow to stop working
options.C: Widespread micro-clotting uses up all clotting factors, leading to severe bleeding
options.D: Rapid clot retraction destroys healthy blood vessel muscle

explanation: DIC is tricky: tiny clots form all over the body first, using up all the clotting proteins. Once those run out, the patient can't form normal clots anymore and starts bleeding massively elsewhere. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h8)
